title: The Scream (1893)
altText: A swirling landscape of wavy orange, red and blue bands with a bridge or path, and a figure in the foreground holding its hands to its face.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement)

context: A work by the Norwegian artist Edvard Munch, dated 1893 on its source page, which lists oil on canvas, tempera and crayon and a collection at the National Gallery in Oslo. The page tags it Allegory, Depression and Fear. Munch made several versions of The Scream.

descriptions.k: Wavy colors fill the sky. A person stands on a path with hands near the face. Everyone has big feelings sometimes. Which colors show a big feeling?
descriptions.g12: Edvard Munch painted wavy orange and blue lines in the sky. A figure holds its hands up near its face. The swirly colors show a big feeling. Everyone has big feelings sometimes. What helps you feel better?
descriptions.g35: Edvard Munch painted The Scream in 1893. The swirling sky and curved lines make the whole scene feel like it is moving with a strong feeling. The page tags it Allegory, Depression and Fear. How do the wavy lines and bright colors help show feelings that are hard to say in words?
descriptions.g68: The Scream (1893) by Edvard Munch is a landmark of Expressionism, in which color and line show inner feeling rather than a calm view. The page tags it Allegory, Depression and Fear, and the Oslo museum holds this version. How do the swirling sky, the sharp diagonal of the path and the simplified figure make anxiety visible?
descriptions.g910: Munch's The Scream (1893) shows how a painter can turn an inner state into a landscape. The swirling bands, bold color and distorted figure make emotion seem to flow through the scene itself. Munch worked on several versions, and the page's Realist label does not match the picture, which is usually placed in Expressionism or Symbolism. How do line and color communicate anxiety, and what makes this image so widely recognized?
descriptions.g1112: The Scream (1893) is usually placed within Expressionism and Symbolism, though the source page's Realist label shows how categories can vary. Edvard Munch translated anxiety into form: the rhythmic sky, the compressed figure and the sharp perspective. The page tags it with Allegory, Depression and Fear. How might the work be read as personal confession, as universal symbol of modern unease, or as a formal experiment, and what limits does the evidence set?

k.daily: Look at the wavy sky. What colors do you see swirling?
k.emotion: Everyone has big feelings sometimes. What big feeling do you think this picture shows?
k.observation: Find the person on the path. What are their hands doing?
k.analysis: Where is the person standing, and what is behind them?
k.line: Trace a wavy line in the sky with your finger. Does it go smoothly?
k.shape: Find a curvy shape in the sky. What does it look like?
k.color: Which colors in The Scream look bright and strong?
k.texture: The sky looks like it is moving. How would it feel if you could touch the swirls?
k.space: Which parts of the painting are close to you, and which are far?
k.light: Where do you see the brightest orange?
k.meaning: What could help the person in the painting feel calmer?
k.culture: This painting is from Norway. What would you tell a friend about it?
k.technique: The painter used swirly lines to show a feeling. How else could you show a feeling with lines?
k.personal: When you have a big feeling, who or what helps you?
k.critical: What would you add to The Scream to make a feeling better?

g12.daily: How do the wavy lines in the sky in The Scream show a big feeling?
g12.emotion: What mood do the colors give you, and which parts make you feel it?
g12.observation: List what you see in the painting, from the person to the sky to the path.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to the person before the swirly sky?
g12.line: How do the long lines of the path and the waves lead your eyes through the painting?
g12.shape: How do the curvy shapes of the sky and the person fit together?
g12.color: How do the bright orange and the dark blue make the painting feel strong?
g12.texture: The paint looks smooth and wavy. How can you tell the painter wanted it to feel like it is moving?
g12.space: How does the path make the picture feel deep, with the person near and the sky far?
g12.light: Where does the light look bright, and where does it look dark?
g12.meaning: Why might the painter have painted a feeling instead of just a place?
g12.culture: What can a painting from Norway in 1893 tell us about how artists showed feelings?
g12.technique: How can an artist use only colors and lines to show a feeling?
g12.personal: What can you do or say when you have a big feeling?
g12.critical: Why do you think so many people know and remember this painting?

g35.daily: Which details in The Scream show a strong feeling even though you cannot hear any sound?
g35.emotion: What feeling do the colors and lines give you, and what supports it?
g35.observation: Study the sky. Where do the waves of color change direction or speed up?
g35.analysis: How does the position of the figure on the path guide your eyes through the picture?
g35.line: How do the curving lines in the sky differ from the straight lines of the path?
g35.shape: How do the simple, rounded shapes of the figure stand out from the swirling background?
g35.color: How do the oranges and reds work with the blues and darks to set the mood?
g35.texture: How does the painter use marks and layers to make the surface feel restless?
g35.space: How does the strong slanted path make the space feel deep and rushing?
g35.light: How does the contrast of bright and dark areas make the scene feel dramatic?
g35.meaning: The page tags the painting Allegory, Depression and Fear. How can a picture show a feeling without telling a story?
g35.culture: What does The Scream tell us about artists in Norway in 1893 who wanted to show inner feelings?
g35.technique: How is painting with swirling lines and strong color different from copying how a place really looks?
g35.personal: What would you ask Edvard Munch about the feeling he painted?
g35.critical: Some people find this painting hard to look at, and others find it helpful. What evidence from the picture supports each view?

g68.daily: How does Munch use the swirling sky and the simplified figure to make an inner feeling visible in The Scream?
g68.emotion: Which choices of color and line make the mood feel urgent rather than calm?
g68.observation: Compare how the figure is painted with how the background is painted. What differences stand out?
g68.analysis: How does the composition use the diagonal path to rush your eye toward the figure?
g68.line: How do the curved bands of the sky contrast with the hard lines of the railing or path?
g68.shape: How does the simplified, almost mask-like figure affect how you read emotion?
g68.color: How does the palette of vivid orange against deep blue create tension?
g68.texture: How do the visible marks and mixed materials, such as tempera and crayon, change the surface of the picture?
g68.space: How does exaggerated perspective create a sense of space that feels unstable?
g68.light: How does the strong contrast of light and dark add to the drama?
g68.meaning: The page lists Allegory, Depression and Fear as tags. How might the painting stand for more than one person's experience?
g68.culture: How might late nineteenth-century Norway and Europe have shaped an artist's interest in inner feelings and modern anxiety?
g68.technique: How does Expressionism differ from realism in what it tries to show, and why does the Realist label on the page not fit?
g68.personal: What emotions would you read in the picture, and how can you respond with care to a painting about distress?
g68.critical: Does a painting about a difficult feeling have to be disturbing to be effective? Use details to explain.

g910.daily: Which formal choices in The Scream convert anxiety into landscape, line and color?
g910.emotion: What emotional register does the work produce, and how do the sky, path and figure shape it?
g910.observation: Examine the treatment of the figure and sky. What does the blending of form reveal about Munch's method?
g910.analysis: How does the steep diagonal of the path and the placement of the figure establish hierarchy and tension?
g910.line: How do the undulating lines of the sky echo the form of the figure, and what does that imply about the relationship between person and world?
g910.shape: How does the simplified, elongated head function as both individual and symbol?
g910.color: How does the clash of saturated oranges with cold blues structure the emotional field?
g910.texture: How does the mixture of oil, tempera and crayon contribute to a raw, unfinished-seeming surface?
g910.space: How does the exaggerated perspective destabilize the viewer's position?
g910.light: How does lighting based on color, not on a single source, change the nature of the drama?
g910.meaning: How do the tags Allegory, Depression and Fear guide interpretation without fixing it?
g910.culture: How does the work fit within the 1890s European interest in psychology and inner life, and where might we avoid overclaiming about the painter's own state of mind?
g910.technique: Why might the page's Realist label be considered inaccurate, and what does that show about how movement labels are used?
g910.personal: What does the painting make you consider about how we communicate feelings that are hard to name?
g910.critical: To what extent has the painting's fame as an icon changed how people see it, and how might you look at it freshly?

g1112.daily: How does the fusion of subjective feeling and observed setting allow The Scream to support readings as personal confession, universal symbol and formal experiment?
g1112.emotion: Might the viewer's sense of anxiety come from the painting's forms or from its reputation? Weigh the visual evidence.
g1112.observation: Scan the junctions where figure, path and sky blend. How do these thresholds shape your sense of whether the distress is inside the person, outside, or both?
g1112.analysis: How does the diagonal composition produce a rush toward the foreground without a conventional narrative?
g1112.line: How do the sky's rhythmic contours relate to the figure's outline, and what does this say about boundaries between self and world?
g1112.shape: In what ways does the near-abstract treatment of the head resist portraiture while preserving human presence?
g1112.color: How does the color structure serve emotional intensity rather than description?
g1112.texture: How does the coexistence of media, as the page lists oil, tempera and crayon, complicate the idea of a single finished surface?
g1112.space: How does the exaggerated perspective challenge the illusionistic space inherited from earlier painting?
g1112.light: How does the non-naturalistic light contribute to the painting's sense of psychic rather than physical atmosphere?
g1112.meaning: How do the page's tags Allegory, Depression and Fear sit alongside scholarly emphasis on Expressionism and Symbolism, and what does the mismatch with the page's Realist label teach us about categories?
g1112.culture: How do the multiple versions of The Scream, as widely known, shape debates about originality and the meaning of an image?
g1112.technique: How does the painting's afterlife in popular culture influence our ability to see it as a historical work?
g1112.personal: How does your own experience of anxiety, or lack of it, shape your response, and how can you engage with the work thoughtfully and with care for others in the room?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that The Scream is better understood as a formal innovation than as a portrait of emotion, and how would you counter it?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium (oil on canvas, tempera and crayon as listed), year (1893), collection (National Gallery, Oslo) and page tags (Allegory, Depression, Fear) read from the arthistoryproject.com page text. SENSITIVE: subject is anxiety and distress; K-2 questions are gentle and focus on big feelings and what helps, avoiding frightening language; older bands treat the theme with care and avoid claims about the artist's own mental health. The page labels the movement Realist, which is inaccurate for this picture; the accepted labels Expressionism (also linked with Symbolism) are used, and this discrepancy is noted here for a reviewer. Only page text was read; the image file was not visually inspected, and a person must view it and confirm it is suitable, with a plan for sensitive conversations, before release.

teacherNote.context: A work from 1893 by Edvard Munch, held by the National Gallery in Oslo, and one of several versions he made. It is often linked with Expressionism and Symbolism, and its tags Depression and Fear call for careful, supportive discussion.
directions: Have students use only lines and colors to draw a feeling (not a scene), then compare and discuss.
Ask students to describe what helps them when they have a big feeling, linking to school supports as appropriate.
Discuss how artists turn inner feelings into pictures; check in gently with students who find the topic hard.
